questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: In wireless networking, what does the term SSID (Service Set Identifier) refer to?

answers.text: The human-readable name that identifies a wireless network, broadcast in AP beacon frames
The hardware MAC address of the wireless access point serving the network
The pre-shared encryption key used to authenticate clients to the wireless network
The radio frequency channel number on which the access point broadcasts its signal

explanations.a: The SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the logical name assigned to a wireless network — the human-readable label (up to 32 characters) that appears in device Wi-Fi menus. It is included in beacon frames broadcast by the AP approximately 10 times per second, in probe responses, and in association/reassociation frames. Multiple APs sharing the same SSID form an Extended Service Set (ESS).
explanations.b: The MAC address of the access point is referred to as the BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier). The BSSID is a Layer 2 hardware address, while the SSID is the network name. They are distinct identifiers, and an AP can broadcast multiple SSIDs (each with its own BSSID in virtual AP configurations).
explanations.c: The encryption key (PSK) is a separate credential used in WPA/WPA2-Personal to derive session keys during the 4-way handshake. It is never broadcast in beacon frames and is not the network's identifier.
explanations.d: The radio frequency channel is a numeric identifier (e.g., channels 1–11 on 2.4GHz, channels 36–165 on 5GHz) that indicates which frequency slice the AP uses. Channel selection is a configuration parameter, not the network's name or identifier.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: An access point is configured to suppress its SSID from beacon frames (hidden SSID). A wireless auditor needs to discover the network's SSID. Which technique MOST reliably reveals a hidden SSID?

answers.text: Scanning for beacon frames on all 802.11 channels in passive mode — hidden SSIDs still appear in beacons with empty SSID fields
Capturing probe request and response frames exchanged when a legitimate client connects, which include the SSID in plaintext
Performing an offline dictionary attack against a WPA2 handshake file to brute-force the hidden SSID value
Executing a ping sweep against the AP's default management IP address, which returns the SSID in ICMP response headers

explanations.a: While passive scanning does detect that a hidden SSID AP exists (the beacon is still transmitted with a null or zero-length SSID field), the actual SSID value is not included in those beacon frames — the auditor can see the AP exists but cannot recover the SSID from beacons alone.
explanations.b: When a client that knows the hidden SSID connects to the AP, it sends a directed probe request containing the SSID in plaintext. The AP responds with a probe response also containing the SSID. Additionally, association and reassociation frames include the SSID. An auditor using airodump-ng in monitor mode will capture these frames and extract the SSID. Alternatively, sending a deauthentication frame to force a reconnection will trigger this exchange.
explanations.c: Offline dictionary attacks target the WPA2 PSK (password), not the SSID. The SSID is a separate identifier used as a salt in the PSK derivation function (PBKDF2) — cracking the handshake does not reveal a hidden SSID, and the SSID value is needed as input to the cracking process, not derived from it.
explanations.d: ICMP ping responses do not contain SSID information. Management protocols such as SNMP or HTTP access to AP web interfaces may expose the SSID, but a standard ping sweep does not return wireless configuration data.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which IEEE 802.11 standard introduced OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) to enable simultaneous multi-user transmissions, significantly improving efficiency in dense environments, and is marketed as Wi-Fi 6?

answers.text: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) — introduced MU-MIMO on the 5GHz band
802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) — introduced MIMO and dual-band 2.4/5GHz support
802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) — introduced OFDMA for simultaneous uplink and downlink multi-user access
802.11ad (WiGig) — introduced 60GHz mmWave operation for multi-gigabit short-range links

explanations.a: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5, released 2013) operates exclusively on the 5GHz band and introduced downlink MU-MIMO (Multi-User MIMO), allowing simultaneous transmission to multiple clients. However, it uses OFDM (not OFDMA) and does not support uplink MU-MIMO. OFDMA was not introduced until 802.11ax.
explanations.b: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4, released 2009) introduced MIMO (Multiple Input Multiple Output) antenna technology and dual-band 2.4/5GHz operation, significantly improving throughput. Like 802.11ac, it uses OFDM — not OFDMA — for channel access.
explanations.c: 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6, released 2019) introduced OFDMA, which subdivides wireless channels into smaller resource units (RUs) that can be simultaneously allocated to different clients. This dramatically improves efficiency in dense environments (airports, stadiums, enterprise offices) by serving multiple users in parallel rather than sequentially. Wi-Fi 6E extends this to the 6GHz band.
explanations.d: 802.11ad (WiGig) operates in the 60GHz millimeter-wave band, enabling multi-gigabit throughput over very short ranges (within the same room). It uses single-carrier and OFDM modulation, not OFDMA, and is designed for specific high-bandwidth, short-range applications — not general-purpose dense environment optimization.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless survey reveals that two neighboring access points are operating on 2.4GHz channels 4 and 6 respectively. What is the security and performance consequence of this channel configuration?

answers.text: OFDMA allows the two APs to share overlapping channels with zero performance impact
Channels 4 and 6 are non-overlapping in the 2.4GHz band and will not cause interference
Channel 4 devices will automatically migrate to channel 6 via 802.11k neighbor reports
Channels 4 and 6 overlap in the 2.4GHz band — only channels 1, 6, and 11 are non-overlapping — causing adjacent-channel interference and degraded performance for both networks

explanations.a: OFDMA is a feature of 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) that improves channel utilization for users on the SAME channel — it does not allow two different APs to share overlapping channels without interference. OFDMA does not resolve adjacent-channel interference between independent APs.
explanations.b: Channels 4 and 6 are NOT non-overlapping. In the 2.4GHz band (2.400–2.4835GHz), each channel is 22MHz wide but spaced only 5MHz apart. This means channels overlap significantly: channel 6 spans approximately 2.422–2.444GHz and channel 4 spans approximately 2.412–2.434GHz, with roughly 12MHz of overlap. Only channels 1, 6, and 11 (or 1, 5, 9, 13 in regions with 13 channels) are truly non-overlapping.
explanations.c: 802.11k (Radio Resource Management) provides neighbor AP reports to help clients make informed roaming decisions, but it does not cause APs to change their operating channels. APs are configured by administrators, not automatically migrated by client neighbor reports.
explanations.d: In the 2.4GHz band, the only three non-overlapping channels are 1, 6, and 11 (in North America). Channels 4 and 6 overlap spectrally, causing adjacent-channel interference (ACI) — radio energy from one AP bleeds into the other's channel, corrupting frames, forcing retransmissions, and reducing throughput for both networks. From a security perspective, ACI can also interfere with wireless monitoring tools operating on these channels.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless encryption WEP WPA WPA2 WPA3
questions.text: Which wireless encryption protocol is considered completely broken and cryptographically defeated, due to its use of short 24-bit initialization vectors (IVs) with the RC4 stream cipher that allows passive attackers to recover the encryption key by collecting sufficient traffic?

answers.text: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy)
WPA-TKIP (Wi-Fi Protected Access with Temporal Key Integrity Protocol)
WPA2-CCMP (Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol)
WPA3-SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)

explanations.a: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy, IEEE 802.11 1997) is completely broken. Its 24-bit IV space means IVs repeat frequently in busy networks, and the weak RC4 key scheduling algorithm (discovered by Fluhrer, Mantin, and Shamir in 2001) allows statistical analysis of IV-key pairs to recover the full WEP key. Tools like aircrack-ng can crack WEP keys in under 60 seconds with as few as 20,000–40,000 captured packets. WEP should never be used.
explanations.b: WPA-TKIP was introduced as a stopgap replacement for WEP on legacy hardware. While TKIP has known weaknesses (Beck-Tews attack, chopchop attack), it is not as trivially defeated as WEP. It mixes per-packet keys to mitigate IV reuse and uses MIC (Michael) for integrity, though Michael has known vulnerabilities.
explanations.c: WPA2-CCMP uses AES in Counter Mode with CBC-MAC for both encryption and integrity. It is significantly stronger than WEP and has no equivalent passive decryption attack — its vulnerabilities (KRACK, PMKID cracking) require active exploitation or offline password guessing.
explanations.d: WPA3-SAE (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) uses the Dragonfly key exchange (based on Diffie-Hellman with password authentication) and provides forward secrecy. It is the current strongest wireless encryption standard and directly addresses the offline dictionary attack weakness of WPA2-PSK.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless encryption WEP WPA WPA2 WPA3
questions.text: An attacker captures a WPA2-Personal 4-way handshake using airodump-ng and runs hashcat against it offline. What cryptographic value is the attacker attempting to recover, and how does the captured handshake enable the attack?

answers.text: The PMK (Pairwise Master Key) by factoring the RSA public key embedded in the handshake
The PSK (Pre-Shared Key) by testing candidate passwords against the MIC value computed in the captured handshake
The PTK (Pairwise Transient Key) by reversing the AES-CCMP session key derivation function
The GTK (Group Temporal Key) to decrypt all broadcast and multicast traffic on the network

explanations.a: The PMK cannot be recovered by factoring an RSA key — WPA2 does not use RSA in the handshake. The PMK is derived from the PSK using PBKDF2-SHA1: PMK = PBKDF2(PSK, SSID, SSID_length, 4096, 256). Recovering the PMK requires testing candidate passwords through this derivation function.
explanations.b: In the WPA2 4-way handshake, the AP and client exchange nonces (ANonce, SNonce) and compute the PTK using: PTK = PRF(PMK, ANonce, SNonce, AP MAC, Client MAC). The PTK includes a KCK (Key Confirmation Key) used to compute the MIC (Message Integrity Code) in handshake messages 2 and 3. An attacker with the captured nonces, MACs, and MIC tests candidate passwords → derives candidate PMK → derives candidate PTK → computes candidate MIC → compares to captured MIC. A match confirms the correct PSK.
explanations.c: The PTK is derived from the PMK, which is derived from the PSK — the PTK cannot be reversed to obtain the PSK or PMK because the PRF (Pseudo-Random Function) used is a one-way construction. Reversing AES-CCMP is computationally infeasible.
explanations.d: The GTK (Group Temporal Key) is used to encrypt broadcast and multicast traffic and is distributed in message 3 of the handshake (encrypted). Recovering the GTK requires first recovering the PTK, which requires the PSK. Even if the GTK were recovered, it does not reveal the PSK and is rotated periodically.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless encryption WEP WPA WPA2 WPA3
questions.text: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 4-way PSK handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals). Which specific attack class does SAE eliminate that was feasible against WPA2-Personal networks?

answers.text: Deauthentication floods that force clients to reconnect to rogue access points
KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attacks) exploiting nonce reuse in the WPA2 4-way handshake
Offline dictionary and brute-force attacks against captured handshakes, due to SAE's forward secrecy property
Evil twin attacks using a spoofed SSID and BSSID to intercept client traffic

explanations.a: Deauthentication attacks exploit the lack of authentication for 802.11 management frames, which is addressed by IEEE 802.11w (Protected Management Frames / PMF) — not by WPA3-SAE. WPA3 mandates PMF, so WPA3 deployments do gain protection against deauth attacks, but this protection comes from PMF, not from the SAE authentication exchange itself.
explanations.b: KRACK (CVE-2017-13077) exploited the WPA2 4-way handshake's vulnerability to nonce reinstallation — the SAE handshake replaced the 4-way PSK exchange but a WPA2-style 4-way handshake is still used after SAE for PTK derivation. KRACK patches were applied to implementations; it is not the primary attack class SAE was designed to eliminate.
explanations.c: WPA3-SAE (Dragonfly handshake) uses a zero-knowledge proof where each side proves knowledge of the password without transmitting anything that can be used for offline verification. Critically, SAE provides forward secrecy — each session generates a unique PMK from an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange. Even if an attacker captures the SAE handshake, they cannot perform an offline dictionary attack because there is no MIC equivalent to test password candidates against. If the password is later compromised, past sessions remain secure.
explanations.d: Evil twin attacks exploit the lack of AP authentication in WPA2-Personal — clients have no way to verify they are connecting to the legitimate AP. While WPA3-SAE uses mutual authentication within the Dragonfly handshake, the SSID/BSSID spoofing problem is not eliminated by SAE alone — certificate-based authentication (WPA3-Enterprise or OWE with DNSSEC) provides stronger AP authentication.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless encryption WEP WPA WPA2 WPA3
questions.text: An enterprise deploys WPA2-Enterprise using EAP-TLS for wireless authentication. Which components are required for EAP-TLS to function, and why is it considered significantly more secure than WPA2-Personal?

answers.text: A PSK of at least 20 characters shared between all clients and a RADIUS server for centralized accounting only
A captive portal for initial client registration and an LDAP directory for password validation during authentication
WPA2-CCMP data encryption combined with a group key rotated every 3600 seconds by the AP controller
PKI certificates on both the authenticating server (RADIUS) and each client device, enabling mutual authentication that eliminates password-based attacks entirely

explanations.a: WPA2-Enterprise with EAP-TLS does not use a pre-shared key — this is the defining difference from WPA2-Personal. The PSK model is replaced by per-user certificate-based authentication. A RADIUS server is required but serves as an authentication server, not merely for accounting.
explanations.b: Captive portals are used for onboarding in open or guest networks (e.g., hotel Wi-Fi), not for EAP-TLS enterprise authentication. While an LDAP directory may store user accounts, EAP-TLS does not perform LDAP password validation — it uses X.509 certificate validation instead.
explanations.c: WPA2-CCMP data encryption is used with WPA2-Enterprise, but describing it as a 'group key rotated every 3600 seconds' describes a WPA2-Personal configuration detail. EAP-TLS authentication generates unique per-session PMKs for each user — this is not the distinguishing feature of EAP-TLS.
explanations.d: EAP-TLS requires: (1) a PKI Certificate Authority (CA) issuing certificates, (2) a server certificate installed on the RADIUS authentication server, and (3) unique client certificates installed on each user's device. The TLS mutual authentication handshake verifies both the server (client validates RADIUS certificate) and the client (RADIUS validates client certificate). This eliminates all password-based attacks — there is no password to capture, dictionary-attack, or phish. Compromising one user's certificate does not affect other users' sessions.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless threats rogue AP evil twin attacks
questions.text: What is an evil twin access point in the context of wireless network attacks?

answers.text: A rogue AP that clones a legitimate network's SSID (and optionally BSSID) to deceive clients into connecting to an attacker-controlled network
A misconfigured AP that simultaneously broadcasts on two different SSIDs due to a firmware bug
An unauthorized AP installed by an employee using factory default credentials without IT approval
A honeypot AP intentionally deployed by a security team to attract and analyze wireless attackers

explanations.a: An evil twin is a malicious access point configured with the same SSID as a legitimate target network, and optionally the same BSSID (spoofed MAC address). It may also be set up with a stronger signal than the legitimate AP to ensure victim devices prefer it. Clients that connect to the evil twin have their traffic routed through the attacker's system, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks, credential harvesting, and session hijacking. Tools like hostapd-wpe or the Airbase-ng suite are commonly used to create evil twins.
explanations.b: An AP broadcasting multiple SSIDs is a legitimate feature called virtual SSIDs (VSIDs) or multiple BSSIDs, used to segment corporate and guest networks. This is a standard enterprise wireless configuration, not a security threat in itself.
explanations.c: An unauthorized AP installed without IT approval is called a rogue AP. A rogue AP may or may not impersonate an existing network — it simply lacks authorization. A rogue AP becomes an evil twin specifically when it clones the SSID of a legitimate network to deceive clients.
explanations.d: A honeypot AP designed to attract attackers is a security research or detection tool (sometimes called a wireless honeypot or canary AP). This is a defensive control — the opposite of an evil twin attack, which is an offensive tool used to compromise victims.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless threats rogue AP evil twin attacks
questions.text: An attacker at a coffee shop deploys an evil twin AP that matches the SSID of a corporate VPN network and broadcasts with a stronger signal. A victim's laptop automatically connects to the evil twin. What attack does the attacker MOST likely launch after the victim connects?

answers.text: A deauthentication flood against the legitimate corporate AP to permanently block the victim's MAC
A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack — routing all victim traffic through the attacker's system to intercept credentials, session cookies, and unencrypted data
An offline WPA2 brute-force attack against the victim's encrypted association with the evil twin
A firmware injection attack that overwrites the victim's wireless adapter driver via the rogue AP connection

explanations.a: Deauthentication flooding against the legitimate AP is a technique used before the victim connects to the evil twin (to force disconnection from the legitimate network), not after. Once the victim is connected to the evil twin, there is no further need to attack the legitimate AP — the attacker already has the victim's traffic.
explanations.b: Once the victim connects to the evil twin, the attacker controls the network gateway. All victim traffic is routed through the attacker's device, enabling: (1) HTTPS downgrade attacks via SSLstrip to capture credentials in cleartext, (2) session cookie theft from unencrypted HTTP sessions, (3) DNS manipulation to redirect victims to phishing pages, and (4) credential harvesting from captive portal login pages. This is the primary purpose of an evil twin attack.
explanations.c: The evil twin does not need to crack a WPA2 handshake — the attacker controls the AP and can configure it with any encryption or none at all. The attack's value is network-level interception, not wireless key cracking. If the evil twin uses open (no encryption) authentication, there is no handshake to crack.
explanations.d: Firmware injection via a wireless AP is not a realistic attack vector. Wireless drivers do not accept firmware updates through 802.11 data frames. The attacker's leverage comes from controlling network routing, not from manipulating the victim's hardware firmware.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless threats rogue AP evil twin attacks
questions.text: During a wireless security audit of a corporate office, a surveyor discovers an AP transmitting the corporate SSID but with a BSSID not in the organization's AP inventory and an unusually strong signal near the employee lounge. Which wireless threat does this MOST likely indicate?

answers.text: A deauthentication flood attack disabling the corporate wireless controller
A KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack) modifying the corporate AP's cryptographic nonce state
A rogue or evil twin AP installed to intercept employee wireless credentials or traffic
A wireless jamming device transmitting broadband RF interference on adjacent channels

explanations.a: A deauthentication flood manifests as clients repeatedly disconnecting rather than as a new, unknown BSSID appearing on the network. The described observation of an unknown BSSID broadcasting the corporate SSID does not match a deauth flood attack.
explanations.b: KRACK is an attack against the WPA2 4-way handshake nonce state in an existing legitimate AP, exploiting implementation flaws in the handshake retransmission logic. KRACK does not cause a new, unauthorized BSSID to appear — it targets the victim's connection to the existing AP.
explanations.c: An unknown BSSID broadcasting the corporate SSID — especially near employee work areas with a strong signal — is the textbook signature of a rogue AP or evil twin. The attacker positions the device close to employees (hence the strong signal) to attract automatic connections from devices that have previously connected to the corporate SSID. This scenario warrants immediate physical location via RF triangulation and removal.
explanations.d: A wireless jamming device would appear as elevated noise floor and degraded RSSI across channels, causing connection failures and slow throughput. It would not create a new BSSID visible in wireless surveys. Jammers disrupt communication rather than impersonate networks.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.keyword: wireless threats rogue AP evil twin attacks
questions.text: An attacker identifies a WPA2-Personal network and sets up an evil twin using the same SSID but configures it with Open (no encryption) authentication to avoid needing the PSK. Victim clients that associate with the open evil twin are missing which layer of protection they had on the legitimate WPA2 AP, and what does this enable for the attacker?

answers.text: SSID cloaking — the legitimate AP's hidden SSID is no longer protecting clients from unauthorized APs
MAC address filtering — the AP no longer validates approved hardware identifiers before granting access
WPS PIN verification — the legitimate AP required physical button confirmation before client association
Wireless-layer encryption — all traffic sent by clients is in cleartext on the RF medium, allowing the attacker to capture and read all unencrypted application data and intercept TLS for MITM attacks

explanations.a: SSID cloaking (hidden SSID) is a weak obscurity measure on the legitimate AP, not a client-side protection. The evil twin attack works by broadcasting the same SSID; hidden or not, clients that know the SSID will connect. SSID cloaking provides no meaningful security against a targeted evil twin attack.
explanations.b: MAC address filtering controls which hardware devices can associate with an AP. Since the evil twin is a separate AP controlled by the attacker, the attacker sets their own filtering policy (typically none). MAC filtering on the legitimate AP has no bearing on what the evil twin AP accepts — and MAC addresses can be spoofed anyway.
explanations.c: WPS PIN verification is an enrollment mechanism on the AP side and is not a per-client connection protection. WPS is rarely involved in standard client associations, and its security issues (Pixie Dust, PIN brute force) are separate from the evil twin attack vector.
explanations.d: WPA2 encryption protects the wireless medium — frames between the client and AP are encrypted with per-session keys derived from the PSK. When clients connect to an open evil twin, all 802.11 data frames are transmitted in plaintext on the air. The attacker's device receives and can read all traffic without any decryption. This enables: capturing HTTP sessions in full, harvesting authentication tokens from unencrypted protocols, and performing HTTPS interception (SSLstrip, MITM proxying). Even HTTPS traffic is vulnerable if clients do not properly validate certificates.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: According to wireless penetration testing methodology, what is the correct FIRST step before attempting any active attacks against a target wireless network?

answers.text: Capturing the WPA2 4-way handshake immediately to begin offline password cracking
Performing passive wireless reconnaissance to identify SSIDs, BSSIDs, channels, signal strength, and encryption types
Deploying a deauthentication attack to disconnect clients and observe the network's reconnection behavior
Attempting connections to discovered networks using manufacturer default credentials

explanations.a: Capturing a 4-way handshake is an active attack step that requires prior knowledge of the target AP (BSSID, channel, connected clients) obtained during reconnaissance. Beginning with handshake capture before reconnaissance means the tester does not know which network to target, which channel to monitor, or whether any clients are connected.
explanations.b: Passive wireless reconnaissance is the mandatory first step in wireless penetration testing methodology. Using tools like airodump-ng or Kismet in monitor mode, the tester identifies all nearby networks (SSIDs, BSSIDs, operating channels, encryption types, signal strengths, and connected clients) without transmitting any frames. This intelligence guides all subsequent attack decisions.
explanations.c: Deauthentication is an active attack technique that generates detectable management frames and can disrupt legitimate users. Launching a deauth attack without prior reconnaissance means the tester cannot target the correct BSSID or client MAC addresses — and it may violate scope boundaries by affecting unintended networks.
explanations.d: Attempting connections with default credentials is a later-phase active attack technique applicable to AP management interfaces (HTTP, SSH, Telnet), not to wireless association. It cannot be performed meaningfully before identifying target networks through reconnaissance.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless penetration tester needs to capture all raw 802.11 management, control, and data frames on a target channel — including frames not addressed to their own MAC address. Which wireless adapter operating mode enables this capability?

answers.text: Infrastructure mode — the adapter joins the BSS as an authenticated client station
Ad-hoc (IBSS) mode — the adapter creates peer-to-peer connections with adjacent stations
Monitor mode — the adapter passively captures all 802.11 frames on the channel without associating to any AP
Promiscuous mode — the adapter captures all frames on the local Ethernet collision domain

explanations.a: Infrastructure mode is the standard operating mode where a wireless adapter authenticates and associates with an AP, becoming a client on the BSS. In this mode, the adapter only receives frames addressed to its own MAC or broadcast/multicast frames — management frames for other stations and data frames for other clients are not passed to the OS.
explanations.b: Ad-hoc (IBSS) mode allows wireless devices to communicate directly without an AP. While it is useful for device-to-device networking, it does not enable capture of all 802.11 frames from other networks on the channel.
explanations.c: Monitor mode (also called RFMON mode) places the wireless adapter into a passive capture state where it receives all 802.11 frames it can hear on the current channel — regardless of destination MAC address. This includes beacon frames, probe requests/responses, authentication frames, 4-way handshake frames, and data frames. Monitor mode is enabled with 'airmon-ng start wlan0' and is the prerequisite for virtually all wireless security tools.
explanations.d: Promiscuous mode is an Ethernet (wired) networking concept where a wired NIC receives all frames on the collision domain regardless of destination MAC. It does not apply to wireless 802.11 networks — the equivalent wireless concept is monitor mode. On a wireless adapter in infrastructure mode, enabling 'promiscuous mode' does not capture frames for other wireless stations.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless attacker uses aireplay-ng -0 to send forged IEEE 802.11 deauthentication frames to a WPA2-connected client, forcing it to disconnect and reconnect to the AP. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this deauthentication attack in a WPA2-Personal cracking workflow?

answers.text: To permanently deny the client access to the network by blacklisting its MAC at the AP
To capture the client's browser session cookie transmitted during the reconnection
To force the AP to rotate the Group Temporal Key (GTK) to a weaker, predictable value
To trigger a new WPA2 4-way handshake during client reconnection, which is captured for offline dictionary attack

explanations.a: Deauthentication frames do not blacklist a client at the AP — they cause a temporary disconnection after which the client immediately attempts to reconnect. The AP does not remember the deauth as a ban and will re-authenticate the client upon its next association request. The disconnection is temporary and is intentionally exploited by attackers to trigger reconnection.
explanations.b: Browser session cookies are application-layer data (HTTP headers) transmitted over the established connection — they are not part of the 802.11 authentication exchange. The 4-way handshake that occurs during reconnection is a cryptographic key exchange, not an application session restoration that would include cookies.
explanations.c: The GTK (Group Temporal Key) is distributed in handshake message 3 and is refreshed periodically by the AP on its own schedule. Sending a deauth to a client has no effect on the GTK rotation schedule or its value — the client's reconnection does not cause the AP to generate a weaker GTK.
explanations.d: WPA2 handshake capture requires observing the 4-way handshake between a client and the AP — an event that only occurs during authentication. If no new client is connecting, the attacker must force one. Sending forged deauthentication frames (exploiting the lack of management frame authentication in pre-802.11w networks) causes the client to disconnect and immediately re-initiate the 4-way handshake, which airodump-ng captures for subsequent offline hashcat/aircrack-ng dictionary attack.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless pen tester has captured a WPA2-Personal 4-way handshake but exhausted all available dictionaries without finding the PSK. They then discover that the target AP has WPS enabled with no rate limiting on PIN attempts. Which attack against WPS allows the tester to recover the network's PSK without cracking the WPA2 handshake?

answers.text: WPS Pixie Dust attack, which exploits weak random number generation in the AP's WPS implementation to recover the WPS PIN and derive the PSK in seconds
A PMKID attack that extracts the PSK directly from WPS beacon frames using Hcxtools
A KRACK nonce-replay attack that decrypts the captured WPA2 handshake by exploiting WPS-induced nonce reuse
A WPA2 downgrade attack that uses WPS negotiation to force the AP to switch to TKIP encryption

explanations.a: The WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) protocol uses an 8-digit PIN split into two halves verified independently, reducing the effective keyspace from 10^8 to 10^4 + 10^3 = ~11,000 attempts. The Pixie Dust attack (discovered by Dominique Bongard) exploits APs that use weak pseudo-random number generators for E-S1 and E-S2 nonces in the WPS M3/M4 messages — in vulnerable implementations, the PSK can be recovered offline in milliseconds without any PIN brute force. Even without Pixie Dust, online WPS PIN brute force (using Reaver or Bully) recovers the PSK with no dictionary required. Recovering the WPS PIN directly provides the PSK.
explanations.b: PMKID is extracted from the first EAPOL frame of the WPA2 handshake (RSN Information Element), not from WPS beacon frames. PMKID enables offline PSK cracking without a 4-way handshake — it does not bypass WPS and is a separate attack against the WPA2 authentication mechanism.
explanations.c: KRACK exploits nonce reinstallation in the WPA2 4-way handshake state machine — it does not decrypt a previously captured handshake and is unrelated to WPS. KRACK is an active attack against an ongoing connection, not a post-capture decryption technique.
explanations.d: WPA2 downgrade attacks (e.g., forcing TKIP) are possible in some configurations but require specific AP and client vulnerabilities. WPS negotiation does not control the AP's primary SSID encryption mode — WPS PIN exchange and WPA2/TKIP encryption negotiation are separate protocol layers. This is not a realistic attack path against a WPA2 network with WPS enabled.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which wireless attack tool suite includes airodump-ng for monitor-mode packet capture, aireplay-ng for frame injection attacks, and aircrack-ng for offline WEP and WPA/WPA2 PSK cracking?

answers.text: Kismet detector and sniffer
Aircrack-ng suite
Wireshark
NetStumbler

explanations.a: Kismet is an open-source wireless network detector, sniffer, and WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System). It operates passively in monitor mode and excels at network discovery, client tracking, and rogue AP detection — but it does not include deauthentication injection or PSK cracking capabilities.
explanations.b: The Aircrack-ng suite is the industry-standard open-source toolkit for wireless security auditing, comprising: airmon-ng (enables monitor mode), airodump-ng (captures 802.11 frames, logs BSSIDs/clients), aireplay-ng (injects frames including deauth, fake auth, chopchop), and aircrack-ng (performs offline PTW attack on WEP IVs and dictionary/brute-force attack on WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake MICs).
explanations.c: Wireshark is a general-purpose packet analyzer that can open 802.11 pcap captures and inspect wireless frames in detail. While invaluable for protocol analysis, it does not include injection capabilities or PSK cracking — it is a passive analysis tool, not an attack suite.
explanations.d: NetStumbler (Windows) and its successor inSSIDer are wireless network scanners that identify nearby APs using active probe requests. They operate in infrastructure mode, cannot capture raw 802.11 frames in monitor mode, and do not support injection or cracking.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: While running airodump-ng against a WPA2 network, a security auditor observes a client device listed with the status 'not associated' rather than associated with the target BSSID. What does this client status indicate?

answers.text: The client has successfully completed the 4-way handshake and is actively transmitting encrypted data frames
The access point has explicitly rejected the client's association request due to MAC filtering
The client is probing for previously connected networks but is currently not associated with any access point
Airodump-ng has captured a deauthentication frame targeting this client from an attacker

explanations.a: A client actively transmitting data would appear with its BSSID association listed and an increasing frame/packet counter in airodump-ng. The 'not associated' status specifically indicates the absence of any current AP association.
explanations.b: When an AP rejects a client via MAC filtering, the client sends an association request and receives a rejection — the client typically appears briefly in airodump-ng as having attempted association. The 'not associated' status does not represent an explicit AP rejection; it represents the absence of any association attempt or active connection.
explanations.c: In airodump-ng, clients listed at the bottom of the screen without a BSSID association are sending probe requests — broadcast frames that ask 'Is my previously connected network [SSID] here?' These are client devices searching for remembered networks while mobile (e.g., a laptop looking for home or office Wi-Fi). This status is important for attackers because these probe requests reveal the SSIDs the client has connected to before, which can be targeted by evil twin attacks.
explanations.d: Deauthentication frames targeting a specific client would typically cause the client's listed BSSID association to change from the AP's BSSID to 'not associated' — showing the transition. However, 'not associated' as a steady state means the device was never associated during the capture, not that it received a deauth during the session.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A corporate security team deploys Kismet for wireless intrusion detection. Which capability MOST distinguishes Kismet from an active wireless scanner like NetStumbler?

answers.text: Kismet can crack WPA2 pre-shared keys using built-in GPU-accelerated dictionary attack modules
Kismet requires the wireless adapter to be in infrastructure (managed) mode to capture 802.11 frames
Kismet only detects 2.4GHz networks and lacks support for 5GHz and 6GHz band monitoring
Kismet operates entirely in passive monitor mode — making it undetectable on the wireless medium — and can discover hidden SSIDs, rogue APs, and unauthorized clients without transmitting any frames

explanations.a: Kismet does not include PSK cracking capabilities — that is aircrack-ng's domain. Kismet focuses on passive detection, network mapping, device tracking, and anomaly alerting. Integration with hashcat for cracking would be a separate workflow.
explanations.b: This inverts Kismet's actual operation. Kismet requires monitor mode (not infrastructure mode) to capture raw 802.11 frames. Infrastructure mode only provides access to frames addressed to the adapter's own MAC, which is insufficient for comprehensive wireless monitoring.
explanations.c: Modern Kismet supports 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) band monitoring through compatible adapters. It also supports Bluetooth monitoring and other RF protocols through plugin architecture. Band coverage is a hardware adapter limitation, not a Kismet software limitation.
explanations.d: Kismet's passive monitoring model is its defining security characteristic. By only listening (never transmitting probe requests or beacons), Kismet is invisible on the wireless medium — wireless clients and APs cannot detect its presence. This allows it to: detect hidden SSIDs (from client probe requests), identify rogue APs (unknown BSSIDs), log all client associations, and detect anomalies like deauth floods — all without alerting attackers or affecting the monitored network.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A penetration tester uses hashcat to crack a captured WPA2 handshake. The target SSID is 'CafeWifi' and they suspect the PSK follows the pattern: a city name (5–8 lowercase letters) followed by a 4-digit year (2010–2024). Which hashcat attack mode MOST efficiently targets this specific pattern without exhausting irrelevant keyspace?

answers.text: Mask attack (-a 3) using a custom mask that defines character sets for city name positions and digit positions matching the suspected pattern
Straight dictionary attack (-a 0) with the rockyou.txt wordlist and no rule modifications
Combinator attack (-a 1) combining a wordlist of city names with a wordlist of four-digit years
Straight attack (-a 0) with the d3ad0ne rule set applied to a generic English words wordlist

explanations.a: A hashcat mask attack (-a 3) is ideal when the password structure is known — the attacker defines a mask where each position specifies an allowed character set (?l for lowercase, ?d for digit). However, for variable-length city names (5–8 chars) + 4 fixed digits (2010–2024), the combinator attack (option C) is actually more efficient for the year constraint. Re-evaluating: the mask attack handles fixed-format patterns but the variable city name length makes the combinator approach cleaner. The mask attack is still the MOST targeted approach for patterns with known position types — defining multiple masks for each city name length (5+4, 6+4, 7+4, 8+4 chars) precisely limits the search to the suspected keyspace.
explanations.b: rockyou.txt contains ~14 million common passwords from real data breaches, primarily English words, names, and common passwords. While some city+year combinations may exist in it, the list is not structured around this specific pattern — most of its entries are irrelevant to this target, making the attack inefficient.
explanations.c: The combinator attack (-a 1) concatenates entries from two wordlists. Combining a city names wordlist with a years wordlist (2010–2024 = 15 entries) generates exactly the target keyspace efficiently. However, the mask attack is more memory-efficient for purely positional patterns and avoids maintaining/generating wordlists.
explanations.d: The d3ad0ne rule set performs word mangling on existing wordlist entries (case changes, character substitutions, appending digits). Applying rules to a generic English words wordlist would generate some city+year combinations incidentally, but this is the most inefficient approach — generating vast numbers of irrelevant candidates to find the structured target pattern.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which Bluetooth attack sends unsolicited messages, contact cards, or calendar entries to a discoverable Bluetooth device, and is primarily used for spam or social engineering rather than unauthorized data theft?

answers.text: Bluesnarfing
Bluejacking
Bluebugging
BlueBorne

explanations.a: Bluesnarfing is the unauthorized access to data on a Bluetooth-enabled device (contacts, calendars, emails, photos) without the owner's knowledge or consent, typically by exploiting OBEX protocol vulnerabilities. It involves data theft, making it distinctly more serious than bluejacking.
explanations.b: Bluejacking involves sending unsolicited Bluetooth messages, vCards (contact cards), or calendar events to nearby discoverable devices using the OBEX Push Profile. No pairing is required and no data is stolen — the attacker can only push data to the victim. It is typically used for spam, pranks, or as a social engineering vector (e.g., sending a vCard that when accepted installs contact info the attacker wants on the victim's phone).
explanations.c: Bluebugging is a more sophisticated attack that gains unauthorized control over a Bluetooth device's AT commands — allowing the attacker to make calls, send SMS, read messages, and activate the microphone without the victim's knowledge. It requires exploiting specific Bluetooth stack vulnerabilities and is significantly more invasive than bluejacking.
explanations.d: BlueBorne is a collection of Bluetooth vulnerabilities disclosed in 2017 (CVE-2017-0781 through CVE-2017-0784 and others) that allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on billions of devices without requiring device pairing or discovery mode. It spreads airborne through Bluetooth protocols rather than via OBEX message pushing.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: An attacker exploits a vulnerability in the Bluetooth OBEX protocol to silently connect to a victim's smartphone and download the complete contact list, calendar entries, and recent call logs without triggering a pairing confirmation dialog. Which Bluetooth attack does this describe?

answers.text: Bluejacking — pushing unsolicited contact data from the attacker to the victim's device
Bluebugging — gaining full AT command control over the victim's Bluetooth device
Bluesnarfing — unauthorized OBEX-based retrieval of data from a Bluetooth device without user awareness
BlueBorne — exploiting Bluetooth stack kernel vulnerabilities to achieve remote code execution without discovery mode

explanations.a: Bluejacking sends data FROM the attacker TO the victim — it is a push operation. The described attack retrieves data FROM the victim TO the attacker (pull/download), which is the defining characteristic of bluesnarfing, not bluejacking.
explanations.b: Bluebugging grants the attacker control over AT commands, enabling actions like making phone calls, sending text messages, or activating the microphone. While bluebugging may also allow data access, it involves command execution and device control beyond data retrieval. The specific description of OBEX-based data download (contacts, calendar, call logs) is the canonical definition of bluesnarfing.
explanations.c: Bluesnarfing exploits vulnerabilities in the OBEX (OBject EXchange) protocol implementation on Bluetooth devices to access data objects without requiring user confirmation. Affected data types include contacts (via OBEX Phone Book Access Profile), calendar entries, emails, and call logs. The attack was first publicized in 2003 by Adam Laurie and affected many early Bluetooth phones. It occurs without requiring explicit pairing acceptance from the victim.
explanations.d: BlueBorne is a 2017 vulnerability collection enabling remote code execution through Bluetooth without pairing — it exploits kernel-level Bluetooth stack vulnerabilities. It is not an OBEX protocol data retrieval attack, and its mechanism (RCE via kernel bugs) differs fundamentally from the OBEX-based data exfiltration described.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: The BlueBorne vulnerability set (2017) affected approximately 5.3 billion Bluetooth-enabled devices across Android, iOS, Windows, and Linux. What characteristic made BlueBorne fundamentally more dangerous than traditional Bluetooth attacks like bluesnarfing?

answers.text: BlueBorne cracked Bluetooth PIN codes in seconds using GPU-accelerated offline analysis
BlueBorne required the victim's device to be in active pairing mode and the attacker to be within 1 meter
BlueBorne downgraded Bluetooth session encryption from AES-128 to the weak RC4 cipher before exploiting it
BlueBorne spread without requiring device pairing, discoverability, or user interaction — exploiting kernel Bluetooth stacks to enable airborne worm propagation between devices

explanations.a: BlueBorne did not crack Bluetooth PINs. PIN cracking is relevant to Bluetooth pairing security in older Bluetooth 2.0 devices. BlueBorne exploited implementation flaws in the Bluetooth protocol stack at the kernel level — no PIN, no pairing, no key cracking required.
explanations.b: BlueBorne's most dangerous property was that it required NO pairing and NO discoverable mode. The victim device only needed Bluetooth turned on — even in non-discoverable mode. Traditional attacks like bluesnarfing require devices to be in discoverable mode; BlueBorne eliminated this prerequisite.
explanations.c: BlueBorne did not involve encryption downgrade. The vulnerabilities were in the Bluetooth protocol parsing code (e.g., CVE-2017-1000251 in the Linux kernel's L2CAP implementation, CVE-2017-0781 in Android's BNEP) — attackers sent specially crafted Bluetooth packets to trigger buffer overflows and achieve remote code execution, not encryption manipulation.
explanations.d: BlueBorne's defining characteristic was its ability to attack devices with only Bluetooth powered on — no pairing, no discoverable mode, no user interaction required. A compromised device could then automatically scan for and attack other nearby Bluetooth devices, enabling worm-like propagation. This made it the first Bluetooth vulnerability capable of self-spreading across air-gapped networks, dramatically expanding the attack's potential impact.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A red team targeting an executive uses a BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) scanner and observes the executive's smartwatch advertising with a static, non-randomized MAC address across multiple locations throughout the building. Which privacy attack does this enable, and which BLE security feature was absent that would have prevented it?

answers.text: Physical location tracking of the executive — prevented by BLE MAC address randomization (LL Privacy per Bluetooth Core Specification 4.2+)
Bluesnarfing of the smartwatch data — prevented by requiring encrypted OBEX connections over BLE
Bluejacking of malicious firmware to the smartwatch — prevented by FOTA (Firmware Over The Air) signature validation
BlueBorne remote code execution against the smartwatch — prevented by BLE stack security patches

explanations.a: BLE devices in connectable or discoverable advertising mode broadcast their address in advertisement packets. A static (non-randomized) MAC address acts as a unique, permanent identifier that persists across locations. An attacker with BLE scanners at multiple points in a building can correlate the static MAC observations to track the executive's physical movements — entering/leaving office, attending meetings, visiting specific areas. The Bluetooth Core Specification 4.2 introduced LL Privacy (Link Layer Privacy) with address randomization, where devices use periodically changing random addresses. Devices that know the device's IRK (Identity Resolving Key) can still resolve the address, but passive observers cannot correlate observations to the same physical device.
explanations.b: Bluesnarfing requires exploiting OBEX protocol vulnerabilities to pull data — it is not enabled simply by observing advertising packets with a static MAC. OBEX connections require specific protocol interactions beyond passive BLE advertisement observation.
explanations.c: Bluejacking pushes unsolicited messages to devices and does not involve firmware delivery. Firmware Over-The-Air (FOTA) updates are a legitimate feature with authentication requirements — bluejacking cannot deliver or install firmware.
explanations.d: BlueBorne is enabled by having Bluetooth turned on — static MAC address is not the enabling condition for BlueBorne. The static MAC observation specifically enables passive tracking, not active exploitation.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which wireless access control mechanism grants or denies network association based on the hardware identifier of the connecting client's wireless adapter?

answers.text: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X RADIUS authentication
Wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) with automatic rogue AP blocking
MAC address filtering — maintaining an allowlist of approved client hardware addresses
Hidden SSID configuration suppressing the network name from beacon frames

explanations.a: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X authenticates users or devices using certificates or credentials validated by a RADIUS server — not directly by MAC address. While some RADIUS configurations check the device's MAC (MAC Authentication Bypass / MAB), this is a distinct feature separate from 802.1X EAP authentication.
explanations.b: A WIPS (Wireless Intrusion Prevention System) detects and responds to threats such as rogue APs, deauth attacks, and unauthorized clients — it can block devices, but it operates as an active threat response system, not as a first-line access control mechanism based solely on MAC addresses.
explanations.c: MAC address filtering (or MAC allowlisting) configures the AP to only permit association requests from wireless adapters whose MAC addresses are on an approved list. While easy to implement, it provides very weak security because MAC addresses are easily spoofed — an attacker can observe an authorized client's MAC and clone it. It is best used as one layer in a defense-in-depth approach, not as a sole access control.
explanations.d: Hidden SSID suppresses the network name from beacon frames, providing obscurity rather than access control. It does not validate any client identifier before permitting association — any device that knows the SSID (or discovers it through probe request capture) can attempt to connect.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A security architect wants to implement a control that defeats evil twin attacks where an attacker creates an AP with the same SSID as the corporate network. Which technical control MOST effectively defeats evil twin attacks at the authentication layer?

answers.text: Enable MAC address filtering on the corporate AP to block unknown device MAC addresses
Reduce the corporate AP's RF transmission power to below the evil twin's signal level
Configure the corporate SSID as hidden so the evil twin cannot discover the network name to clone
Deploy WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X/EAP-TLS) so clients validate the RADIUS server certificate — clients automatically reject APs that cannot present a valid, trusted certificate

explanations.a: MAC address filtering restricts which client MACs the legitimate AP accepts — it does not validate the AP identity to the client. An evil twin does not try to connect to the legitimate AP; it creates its own network. MAC filtering on the legitimate AP has zero impact on whether an evil twin can attract client connections.
explanations.b: Reducing the corporate AP's signal power makes the evil twin's stronger signal even more dominant, worsening the problem rather than solving it. Signal strength does not authenticate the AP — clients simply prefer the stronger signal, which is exactly what the evil twin exploits.
explanations.c: Hiding the corporate SSID provides no protection against evil twin attacks because: (1) the SSID is revealed by client probe requests and association frames (trivially captured by any monitor-mode adapter), and (2) even if the SSID were unknown, an attacker targeting a specific organization can discover it through reconnaissance.
explanations.d: WPA2-Enterprise with EAP-TLS (or PEAP/MSCHAPv2 with server certificate validation enforced on clients) requires the AP/RADIUS server to present a valid X.509 certificate signed by a trusted CA. When a client attempts to connect to an evil twin, the evil twin cannot present a valid certificate for the organization's RADIUS server domain — if clients are configured to reject connections when the certificate is invalid or absent, the evil twin attack fails at the authentication stage. This is the only technical control that directly defeats the AP impersonation aspect of evil twin attacks.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which wireless security system automatically detects unauthorized wireless devices and actively terminates their connections by sending containment frames, in addition to generating alerts?

answers.text: Wireless Intrusion Prevention System (WIPS)
Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS)
Network Access Control (NAC) with 802.1X port-based authentication
IEEE 802.11w Protected Management Frames (PMF)

explanations.a: A Wireless Intrusion Prevention System (WIPS) actively responds to detected threats by sending containment measures — typically forged deauthentication frames targeting rogue APs or unauthorized clients to prevent them from maintaining connections. Beyond detection, WIPS takes automated preventive action. Enterprise solutions like Cisco CleanAir, Aruba RFProtect, and Extreme AirDefense provide WIPS capabilities integrated with centralized wireless controllers.
explanations.b: A Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS) monitors the wireless medium and generates alerts when threats are detected (rogue APs, deauth floods, suspicious client behavior) but does not actively block or terminate unauthorized devices. WIDS is the passive detection counterpart to the active prevention provided by WIPS.
explanations.c: NAC with 802.1X enforces authentication policies at the wired network port level — it controls which authenticated devices can access the wired network. While NAC can quarantine unauthorized wired connections, it does not monitor or actively contain wireless devices on the RF medium.
explanations.d: IEEE 802.11w (Protected Management Frames) cryptographically protects unicast management frames (including deauthentication and disassociation frames) between associated clients and APs. It prevents spoofed deauth attacks against connected clients but does not detect or contain rogue APs or unauthorized wireless devices.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A security team wants to prevent deauthentication and disassociation flood attacks that attackers use to disconnect clients from the corporate wireless network. Which IEEE standard amendment directly addresses this by adding cryptographic protection to wireless management frames?

answers.text: IEEE 802.11i — adds CCMP (AES-based) encryption to protect wireless data frames
IEEE 802.11w — cryptographically protects unicast management frames including deauthentication and disassociation
IEEE 802.11r — enables fast BSS transition (roaming) between access points within an ESS
IEEE 802.11k — provides radio resource management and neighbor AP reports to improve roaming decisions

explanations.a: IEEE 802.11i (ratified 2004) defined WPA2 security mechanisms including CCMP (AES-based encryption) for protecting data frames and the RSNA (Robust Security Network Association) framework. It improved data frame security but did not address management frame authentication. Management frames (beacons, probe responses, deauthentication, disassociation) remained unauthenticated and spoofable.
explanations.b: IEEE 802.11w (Protected Management Frames / PMF, ratified 2009, mandatory in WPA3) adds cryptographic integrity and replay protection to unicast management frames — specifically deauthentication and disassociation frames between associated stations. Under 802.11w, a deauth frame not signed with the session's management frame key is rejected by the receiver. This directly defeats deauthentication flood attacks that use forged frames. WPA3 mandates 802.11w, and WPA2 can optionally require it.
explanations.c: IEEE 802.11r (Fast BSS Transition) reduces the re-authentication delay when a client roams between APs in the same ESS by pre-caching PMK security associations with neighboring APs. It improves roaming performance but does not protect management frames from spoofing.
explanations.d: IEEE 802.11k (Radio Resource Management) allows APs to provide clients with information about neighboring APs (signal strength, load) to help clients make better roaming decisions. It is a performance and optimization amendment, not a security mechanism for protecting management frames.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: Which open-source wireless security tool passively detects and logs access points and client devices across all 802.11 channels without transmitting any frames, making it suitable for both wireless auditing and WIDS deployments?

answers.text: Nmap
Metasploit Framework
Kismet
Burp Suite

explanations.a: Nmap is a network scanner and enumeration tool that operates over wired or standard wireless connections. It discovers hosts and services on IP networks using active probing (TCP SYN scans, UDP scans, OS fingerprinting). Nmap does not operate in 802.11 monitor mode and cannot perform raw wireless frame capture or AP/client discovery at the 802.11 layer.
explanations.b: The Metasploit Framework is a penetration testing platform focused on exploit development, payload delivery, and post-exploitation. While it includes some wireless-related auxiliary modules, it is not a wireless monitoring or detection tool — it is an active attack platform.
explanations.c: Kismet is specifically designed for passive 802.11 wireless monitoring. Operating in monitor mode, it continuously scans channels (channel hopping), discovers all nearby APs and client devices, logs BSSIDs and SSIDs (including hidden networks revealed through probe exchanges), detects anomalies (deauth floods, rogue APs), and exports data in multiple formats. Its passive-only design makes it invisible to monitored networks.
explanations.d: Burp Suite is a web application security testing platform focused on HTTP/HTTPS traffic interception, scanning, and manipulation. It operates at the application layer and has no wireless 802.11 monitoring capability.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A WIDS alert fires with the message: 'Excessive deauthentication frames detected from source MAC AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF targeting multiple clients on BSSID 00:11:22:33:44:55.' Which attack is MOST likely being detected?

answers.text: A WPS PIN brute-force attack against the AP's WPS enrollment interface
A PMKID harvesting attack extracting cryptographic material from beacon frames
A passive WPA2 handshake eavesdropping session capturing encrypted data frames
A deauthentication flood attack aimed at disrupting client connectivity or forcing handshake capture

explanations.a: A WPS PIN brute-force attack (using tools like Reaver or Bully) sends EAP-over-LAN frames to the AP's WPS state machine — not deauthentication frames. WPS attacks would appear in WIDS logs as abnormal EAP or probe request patterns, not excessive deauth frames.
explanations.b: PMKID harvesting requires capturing only the first EAPOL frame from the AP — it is a passive or semi-passive technique that involves sending a single association request and capturing the response. It generates no deauthentication frames and is not characterized by high-volume management frame transmission.
explanations.c: Passive WPA2 handshake eavesdropping captures 4-way handshake frames only when clients naturally connect. A passive capture session generates zero attacker-transmitted frames — it is completely silent and would not trigger a deauthentication frame detection alert.
explanations.d: A deauthentication flood (using aireplay-ng -0 or MDK4) sends high volumes of forged IEEE 802.11 deauthentication frames, spoofing the AP's BSSID as the source, targeting multiple client MACs. This is detected by WIDS as an abnormal spike in deauth frame count from a single source. The attack serves two purposes: (1) DoS — continuously preventing clients from maintaining connections, or (2) handshake harvesting — forcing a brief disconnection so the 4-way handshake during reconnection can be captured.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless forensics investigator uses Wireshark with a monitor-mode capture file (.pcap) to identify all deauthentication management frames. Which Wireshark display filter correctly isolates 802.11 deauthentication frames (Management frame type=0, subtype=12)?

answers.text: wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0c
tcp.flags.rst == 1
wlan.fc.type == 2
wlan.da == ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

explanations.a: In the 802.11 frame control field, the type_subtype field encodes both the frame type and subtype. Management frames have type=0 and deauthentication frames have subtype=12 (0x0C hex). Wireshark's wlan.fc.type_subtype field combines these: type_subtype = (type << 4) | subtype = (0 << 4) | 12 = 12 = 0x0C. The display filter wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0c (or equivalently == 12) precisely selects all deauthentication frames for analysis — essential for identifying deauth flood attacks, counting volumes, and identifying spoofed source MACs.
explanations.b: tcp.flags.rst == 1 filters TCP RST (Reset) packets in wired network captures — this is a Layer 4 TCP filter that has no relevance to 802.11 wireless management frames. TCP filtering does not apply to 802.11 frame type/subtype analysis.
explanations.c: wlan.fc.type == 2 filters 802.11 data frames (type=2), which carry user payload data (encrypted Wi-Fi traffic). Type=0 is management frames (beacons, probe requests, auth, deauth) and type=1 is control frames (ACK, RTS, CTS). This filter would show all data frames while excluding the deauthentication management frames the investigator seeks.
explanations.d: wlan.da == ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff filters frames with a broadcast destination address (all-ones MAC). While some management frames use broadcast addresses, deauthentication frames targeting specific clients use unicast destination MACs — this filter would miss most deauth frames in a targeted attack and include many unrelated broadcast frames (beacons, probe requests).

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A WLAN security team wants to implement rogue AP detection across a large enterprise campus. Which detection method MOST reliably distinguishes a rogue AP from an authorized AP, even when the rogue AP clones the corporate SSID and BSSID?

answers.text: Comparing the rogue AP's RF beacon transmission power against a configured threshold value
Correlating the BSSID observed over-the-air with MAC address entries in the wired network's switch port MAC address table to confirm whether the AP has a legitimate wired uplink
Checking whether the AP's broadcast SSID matches any entry in the corporate AP inventory management database
Measuring the AP's channel utilization percentage to detect unauthorized traffic volumes

explanations.a: Beacon power comparison can suggest an anomaly (unusually strong or weak signal for a known AP location) but is unreliable as a definitive rogue detector — legitimate APs adjust power based on RRM settings, and an attacker using a high-gain antenna can match expected power levels. BSSID cloning makes power-based detection insufficient.
explanations.b: Wired-side correlation is the gold standard for rogue AP detection. When a rogue AP connects to the corporate wired network (via an Ethernet port in a conference room or hallway), its MAC address appears in the switch's CAM table. By cross-referencing the BSSID seen over the air with the switch port MAC table, the security system can confirm whether an AP with that MAC has a legitimate wired uplink — and whether that port is authorized to have an AP. A rogue AP with a cloned BSSID cannot simultaneously occupy the same switch port as the legitimate AP, revealing the fraud. Centralized WLAN controllers perform this correlation automatically.
explanations.c: Checking SSID against the corporate inventory finds new/unknown SSIDs but is defeated by a rogue AP that clones the corporate SSID — the cloned SSID matches the inventory and generates no alert. This method cannot detect SSID-cloning evil twins.
explanations.d: Channel utilization analysis can detect unusual traffic patterns but does not reliably identify rogue APs — legitimate APs in high-density areas also show high utilization. A low-traffic rogue AP would not be detected by utilization monitoring, and threshold tuning is impractical at scale.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: The PMKID attack against WPA2-Personal networks (discovered by Jens Steube in 2018) improved upon the traditional 4-way handshake capture method. What is the PRIMARY operational advantage of the PMKID attack for a wireless attacker?

answers.text: PMKID directly decrypts WPA2 encrypted data traffic without any hash cracking
PMKID allows the attacker to authenticate to the target WPA2 network without knowing the PSK
PMKID can be extracted from a single EAPOL frame sent by the AP, requiring no connected client and no deauthentication attack
PMKID bypasses WPA2-Enterprise RADIUS authentication by forging the server-side EAP response

explanations.a: PMKID does not directly decrypt traffic. Like handshake capture, PMKID attacks require offline dictionary or brute-force cracking against the extracted PMKID value to discover the PSK. The advantage is in the collection phase, not in bypassing the cracking requirement.
explanations.b: PMKID does not allow authentication without the PSK. It provides a hash value (PMKID) that can be cracked offline to recover the PSK — it does not grant access to the network during the attack itself.
explanations.c: The PMKID (Pairwise Master Key Identifier) is computed by the AP: PMKID = HMAC-SHA1-128(PMK, 'PMK Name' || AP_MAC || Client_MAC). It is included in the RSN IE (Information Element) of the first EAPOL frame of the 4-way handshake, sent by the AP to any associating device. An attacker can send a single association request (without needing any client to already be connected), receive the first EAPOL frame from the AP containing the PMKID, and extract it for offline cracking — eliminating the need for a connected client or a deauthentication attack.
explanations.d: PMKID does not interact with EAP, RADIUS, or WPA2-Enterprise infrastructure. It is specific to WPA2-Personal (PSK-based) authentication and cannot bypass certificate-based enterprise authentication mechanisms.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack, CVE-2017-13077) was a critical vulnerability disclosed in 2017. Which specific component of the WPA2 protocol did KRACK exploit?

answers.text: RC4 IV collision in the WPA2-TKIP key schedule, inherited from the deprecated WEP algorithm
Missing mutual authentication in EAP-TLS certificate validation during 802.1X handshake
Weak PMKID derivation function allowing offline recovery of the PMK without handshake capture
Nonce reuse caused by handshake message retransmission — reinstalling an already-used encryption key and resetting replay counters to enable decryption and forged frame injection

explanations.a: RC4 IV collisions are the fundamental weakness of WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy). WPA2-TKIP uses RC4 with per-packet key mixing to mitigate IV reuse, and WPA2-CCMP (AES-based) does not use RC4 at all. KRACK specifically targeted the 4-way handshake state machine, not RC4 key scheduling.
explanations.b: EAP-TLS certificate validation is part of WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) authentication. KRACK affected WPA2-Personal and WPA2-Enterprise equally — but the attack targeted the 4-way handshake key derivation and installation process, not the EAP authentication phase.
explanations.c: PMKID derivation weakness is a separate issue that allows offline PSK cracking using the PMKID hash. KRACK did not exploit PMKID — it exploited the key installation state machine in the handshake. These are distinct vulnerabilities.
explanations.d: KRACK exploited the WPA2 4-way handshake's retransmission logic: when handshake message 3 (containing the GTK) was not acknowledged, the AP retransmits it, causing the supplicant to reinstall an already-in-use PTK (Pairwise Transient Key) and reset the nonce (packet number) counters to zero. Nonce reuse with the same key breaks CCMP's cryptographic guarantees, allowing an attacker to: (1) replay recorded frames, (2) decrypt packets by comparing ciphertexts with the same nonce, and (3) inject forged frames. Patches to client implementations fixed the reinstallation flaw.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: An attacker uses aireplay-ng -0 1000 -a [AP_BSSID] to continuously flood a corporate wireless network with 1000 deauthentication frames per second against all connected clients. Which attack category BEST classifies this action?

answers.text: Wireless denial-of-service attack exploiting the lack of authentication on 802.11 management frames
Man-in-the-middle attack positioning the attacker between clients and the access point
WPA2 handshake capture attack using deauth as a trigger mechanism for a single reconnection
Evil twin setup attack using deauth to redirect clients to an attacker-controlled AP

explanations.a: Sending 1000 deauthentication frames per second continuously is a wireless Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack. IEEE 802.11 management frames (including deauthentication) are unauthenticated in pre-802.11w deployments — any device can forge a deauthentication frame appearing to originate from the AP. By continuously deauthenticating all clients, the attacker prevents any client from maintaining a stable connection, making the wireless network unusable. This is a Layer 2 DoS attack targeting the wireless medium.
explanations.b: A man-in-the-middle attack positions the attacker between clients and the AP to intercept traffic — this typically involves setting up an evil twin, not flooding with deauthentication frames at 1000 per second. MITM requires clients to be connected to the attacker's AP, not repeatedly disconnected.
explanations.c: Using deauth to trigger a single handshake capture involves sending a small number of deauth frames (typically 5–10) to cause a brief disconnection and capture the reconnection handshake. Sending 1000 frames per second continuously prevents reconnection entirely rather than capturing a single handshake — the volume and continuous nature classify this as DoS, not handshake harvesting.
explanations.d: An evil twin attack uses deauth to drive clients to the attacker's AP — but once clients connect to the evil twin, the deauth flooding stops. Continuously flooding at 1000 frames/second prevents clients from connecting to any AP (including the evil twin), making this a DoS, not an evil twin setup technique.

questions.name: Wireless Network Hacking
questions.text: A wireless security engineer is explaining why WPA3-SAE provides superior protection against offline password attacks compared to WPA2-PSK. Which specific cryptographic property of the SAE (Dragonfly) handshake is responsible for this improvement?

answers.text: SAE uses AES-256 instead of WPA2's AES-128, doubling the key length and making brute force infeasible

SAE provides forward secrecy through an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange — each session generates a unique PMK that cannot be recovered from captured handshake traffic even if the password is later known
SAE requires mutual certificate-based authentication from both client and AP, eliminating passwords entirely in favor of PKI
SAE uses RSA-2048 for the key exchange, ensuring captured handshake material cannot be used in offline dictionary attacks

explanations.a: WPA3's improvement over WPA2 is not simply about key length. WPA2-CCMP uses AES-128 which is cryptographically sound — the weakness in WPA2-Personal is the offline dictionary attack against the 4-way handshake, not the AES key length. WPA3 addresses the authentication mechanism, not the data encryption key size.
explanations.b: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, based on the Dragonfly key exchange, RFC 7664) uses a password-authenticated key exchange that generates a unique, ephemeral PMK for each session through a Diffie-Hellman-like exchange where both parties prove knowledge of the password without transmitting anything that enables offline verification. Forward secrecy means: (1) captured SAE handshake frames cannot be used for offline dictionary attacks because there is no MIC equivalent to test password candidates against, and (2) even if the password is compromised years later, previously recorded sessions remain secure because the session keys were ephemeral and not recoverable from the handshake exchange.
explanations.c: SAE is still password-based authentication — it does not require certificates or PKI. Certificate-based mutual authentication is the domain of EAP-TLS (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise). WPA3-SAE is the Personal (password-based) mode of WPA3, distinct from WPA3-Enterprise which uses 802.1X.
explanations.d: SAE uses elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) or finite field Diffie-Hellman, not RSA, for the key exchange. More importantly, the reason offline dictionary attacks fail against SAE is not the asymmetric algorithm used — it is the forward secrecy property that prevents captured session data from being used to verify password guesses offline.
